title: Spin-Orbit-Mediated Magnetization Transfer in the Fermi-Hubbard Model
authors: Jialiang Tang, Ruoqian Xu, Gloria Platero, Yue Ban, Xi Chen
abstract: We demonstrate spin--orbit-coupling (SOC) catalysis of magnetization-sector transfer in the half-filled Fermi--Hubbard model. Without SOC, conservation of total magnetization confines the dynamics to the initial sector, preventing an antiferromagnetically correlated state from reaching the polarized ferromagnetic sector under a Zeeman ramp. A transient SOC control lifts this obstruction by coupling otherwise disconnected magnetization sectors and converting symmetry-protected crossings into avoided crossings, thereby opening a finite-gap pathway for magnetic-state conversion. We further accelerate the SOC-enabled dynamics beyond the adiabatic timescale using gradient-ascent pulse engineering (GRAPE) and a variational quantum circuit. Both approaches achieve rapid magnetization transfer in one- and two-dimensional Fermi--Hubbard lattices. Our results establish transient SOC as a controllable catalyst for overcoming symmetry-imposed dynamical constraints, while optimal control sets the timescale for the resulting magnetization-sector transfer.
summary: This work demonstrates that transient spin-orbit coupling (SOC) can act as a catalyst to enable magnetization transfer in the Fermi-Hubbard model, overcoming limitations imposed by symmetry conservation. By applying quantum optimal control techniques like GRAPE, the researchers successfully accelerate this otherwise slow process in both 1D and 2D lattices.
main_problem: The study addresses overcoming symmetry-imposed dynamical constraints that prevent the transfer of magnetization from an antiferromagnetically correlated state to a polarized ferromagnetic sector during a Zeeman ramp.
main_result: Transient spin-orbit coupling (SOC) acts as a controllable catalyst, opening finite-gap pathways for this magnetization-sector transfer, which can be rapidly accelerated using quantum optimal control techniques.
method: The research employs quantum optimal control methods, specifically Gradient-Ascent Pulse Engineering (GRAPE) and Variational Quantum Circuits (VQC), to design time-dependent Hamiltonian controls.
model_or_system: The system is the spinful Fermi-Hubbard (FH) model, studied in 1D and 2D lattices at half-filling. The total Hamiltonian includes hopping, interaction, a Zeeman term, and a time-dependent SOC term.
key_observables: Total magnetization ($\hat{M}$), final connected spin-spin correlations ($S(i, j)$), and the time required for magnetization transfer ($\mu(t)$).
important_parameters: The SOC coupling ($\lambda(t)$) is the key control parameter, alongside the Zeeman ramp $f(t)$. Optimal control significantly reduces the transfer time from adiabatic timescales to much shorter, engineered timescales.
main_assumptions: The SOC control is treated as a normalized pulse envelope inherited from the Zeeman ramp, and the dynamics are analyzed using both time-evolution simulation and mapping to quantum circuits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the control architecture, the sector-transfer mechanism showing gap closing (no SOC) versus avoided crossing (with SOC), and the resulting magnetization dynamics and final spin correlations.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the symmetry constraint in the FH model. It then introduces SOC as a catalyst. The core methodology involves applying quantum optimal control (GRAPE/VQC) to accelerate the transfer, demonstrating success in both 1D and 2D lattices.
why_interesting: The use of SOC as a tunable catalyst to bypass symmetry-protected dynamical bottlenecks is highly relevant for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated quantum materials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Fermi–Hubbard models and control architecture. (a) One-dimensional chain with hopping τx, on-site interaction U, longitudinal Zeeman driving, and SOC-induced spin-flip hopping λx. (b) Two-dimensional lattice with hopping am- plitudes τx,y and SOC strengths λx,y along the two lattice directions. The inset highlights the on-site interaction and SOC-assisted spin-flip process. (c) Trotterized digital rep- resentation of the SOC-assisted dynamics in terms of hop- ping, interaction, Zeeman, and SOC evolution blocks. (d) Quantum–classical variational control loop, where measured observables are used to update the layer-dependent circuit pa- rameters θi.

FIG. 2. (a) Magnetization dynamics along the reference ramp with and without SOC. Solid lines denote Hamiltonian evolu- tion, while symbols show the corresponding digitized dynam- ics. (b) Magnetization quantum number M for the instan- taneous ground state for λ(t) = 0, obtained by exact diag- onalization. (c,d) Instantaneous low-energy excitation spec- trum, En(t)−E0(t) for n = 1, . . . , 6, along the adiabatic path without and with SOC, respectively. Parameters: U = 7, λSOC = 1, and tf = 1200 for the adiabatic reference.

FIG. 3. Optimization of SOC-assisted magnetization-sector transfer in 1D (left column) and 2D (right column) FH sys- tems. (a),(b) Magnetization dynamics for the adiabatic evo- lution, GRAPE optimization, and optimized digital circuit. (c),(d) Final connected spin correlations, showing the conver- sion from antiferromagnetic to predominantly ferromagnetic correlations. (e),(f) GRAPE-optimized Zeeman and SOC am- plitudes fk and λk, with the FH parameters τ and U held fixed. For the 1D chain, NT = 150, δt = 0.2, and tf = 30; for the 2 × 3 lattice, NT = 200, δt = 0.15, and tf = 30.

FIG. 4. Sensitivity to static calibration errors. The normal- ized final magnetization µ(tf) is shown for the adiabatic refer- ence (blue solid), GRAPE-optimized protocol (green dashed), and optimized variational circuit (red dotted) as a function of (a) the Zeeman amplitude error ϵf and (b) the SOC ampli- tude error ϵλ. In each scan, one control amplitude is rescaled while the other is kept at its calibrated value, and the control profiles are not reoptimized.
